n: *Study note:* *Psalm 61*. The psalmist cries out for help and expresses his confidence that God will protect him.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the end of the earth.” This may indicate (1) the psalmist is exiled in a distant land, or (2) it may be hyperbolic (the psalmist feels alienated from God’s presence, as if he were in a distant land).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “while my heart faints.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form here expresses the psalmist’s wish or prayer.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “on to a rocky summit [that] is higher than I.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* Or “have been.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a strong tower from the face of an enemy.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will live as a resident foreigner in your tent permanently.” The cohortative is understood here as indicating resolve. Another option is to take it as expressing a request, “please let me live” (cf. NASB, NRSV).

*Study note:* *I will find shelter in the protection of your wings*. The metaphor compares God to a protective mother bird.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you grant the inheritance of those who fear your name.” “Inheritance” is normally used of land which is granted as an inheritance; here it refers metaphorically to the blessings granted God’s loyal followers. To “fear” God’s name means to have a healthy respect for his revealed reputation which in turn motivates one to obey God’s commands (see {{Psalm 86:11|Ps 86:11}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “days upon days of the king add, his years like generation and generation.”

*Study note:* It is not certain if the (royal) psalmist is referring to himself in the third person in this verse, or if an exile is praying on behalf of the king.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sit [enthroned].” The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive here, expressing the psalmist’s prayer.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “loyal love and faithfulness appoint, let them protect him.”

*Translator's note:* Or “forever.”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “and thereby fulfill.” The preposition with the infinitive construct here indicates an accompanying circumstance.

*Study note:* *Psalm 62*. The psalmist expresses his unwavering confidence in God’s justice and in his ability to protect his people.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “only for God [is] there silence [to] my soul.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from him [is] my deliverance.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my high rocky summit.”

*Translator's note:* Or “my elevated place” (see {{Psalm 18:2|Ps 18:2}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text adds רַבָּה (rabbah, “greatly”) at the end of the line. It is unusual for this adverb to follow a negated verb. Some see this as qualifying the assertion to some degree, but this would water down the affirmation too much (see v. {{Psalm 62:6|6b}}, where the adverb is omitted). If the adverb has a qualifying function, it would suggest that the psalmist might be shaken, though not severely. This is inconsistent with the confident mood of the psalm. The adverb probably has an emphatic force here, “I will not be greatly shaken” meaning “I will not be upended.”

*Translator's note:* The verb form is plural; the psalmist addresses his enemies. The verb הוּת (hut) occurs only here in the OT. An Arabic cognate means “shout at.” Here “man” is a generic reference to the victim of the psalmist’s enemies, but in context it ultimately refers to the psalmist himself. To clarify this, the words “like me” have been supplied in the translation.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has a Pual (passive) form, but the verb form should be vocalized as a Piel (active) form. See BDB 953-54 s.v. רָצַח.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like a bent wall and a broken fence.” The point of the comparison is not entirely clear. Perhaps the enemies are depicted as dangerous, like a leaning wall or broken fence that is in danger of falling on someone (see C. A. Briggs and E. G. Briggs, *Psalms* [ICC], 2:69).

*Translator's note:* That is, the psalmist’s enemies addressed in the previous verse.

*Translator's note:* That is, the generic “man” referred to in the previous verse. The words “their victim” have been supplied in the translation to clarify the referent.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “only from his lofty place [or perhaps, “dignity”] they plan to drive [him] away.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they delight [in] a lie.”

*Study note:* The enemies use deceit to bring down their victim. They make him think they are his friends by pronouncing *blessings* upon him, but inwardly they desire his demise.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “only for God be silent, my soul.” The wording is similar to that of v. {{Psalm 62:1|1a}}. Here an imperatival form, דּוֹמִּי (dommi, “be silent”), appears instead of the noun דּוּמִיָּה (dumiyyah, “silence”). The psalmist is encouraging himself to maintain his trust in God.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for from him [is] my hope.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my high rocky summit.”

*Translator's note:* Or “my elevated place” (see {{Psalm 18:2|Ps 18:2}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “upon God [is] my deliverance and my glory, the high rocky summit of my strength, my shelter [is] in God.”
*Translator's note:* To “pour out one’s heart” means to offer up to God intense, emotional lamentation and petitionary prayers (see Lam 2:19).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “only a breath [are] the sons of mankind, a lie [are] the sons of man.” The phrases “sons of mankind” and “sons of man” also appear together in {{Psalm 49:2|Ps 49:2}}. Because of the parallel line there, where “rich and poor” are mentioned, a number of interpreters and translators treat these expressions as polar opposites, בְּנֵי אָדָם (bene ʾadam) referring to the lower classes and בְּנֵי אִישׁ (bene ʾish) to higher classes. But usage does not support such a view. The rare phrase בְּנֵי אִישׁ (“sons of man”) appears to refer to human beings in general in its other uses (see {{Psalm 4:2|Pss 4:2}}; Lam 3:33). It is better to understand the phrases as synonymous expressions.

*Translator's note:* The noun הֶבֶל (hevel), translated “a breath” earlier in the verse, appears again here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not trust in oppression.” Here “oppression” stands by metonymy for the riches that can be gained by oppressive measures, as the final line of the verse indicates.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and in robbery do not place vain hope.” Here “robbery” stands by metonymy for the riches that can be gained by theft, as the next line of the verse indicates.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[as for] wealth, when it bears fruit, do not set [your] heart [on it].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one God spoke, two which I heard.” This is a numerical saying utilizing the “x” followed by “x + 1” pattern to facilitate poetic parallelism. (See W. M. W. Roth, *Numerical Sayings in the Old Testament* [VTSup], 55-56.) As is typical in such sayings, a list corresponding to the second number (in this case “two”) follows. Another option is to translate, “God has spoken once, twice [he has spoken] that which I have heard.” The terms אַחַת (ʾakhat, “one; once”) and שְׁתַיִם (shetayim, “two; twice”) are also juxtaposed in {{2 Kings 6:10|2 Kgs 6:10}} (where they refer to an action that was done more than “once or twice”) and in {{Job 33:14|Job 33:14}} (where they refer to God speaking “one way” and then in “another manner”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that strength [belongs] to God.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and to you, O Master, [is] loyal love.”

*Study note:* *You repay men for what they do*. The psalmist views God’s justice as a demonstration of both his power (see v. {{Psalm 62:11|11c}}) and his loyal love (see v. {{Psalm 62:12|12a}}). When God judges evildoers, he demonstrates loyal love to his people.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for you pay back to a man according to his deed.” Another option is to understand vv. {{Psalm 62:11|11b}} and {{Psalm 62:12|12a}} as the first principle and v. {{Psalm 62:12|12b}} as the second. In this case one might translate, “God has declared one principle, two principles I have heard, namely, that God is strong, and you, O Lord, demonstrate loyal love, and that you repay men for what they do.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 63*. The psalmist expresses his intense desire to be in God’s presence and confidently affirms that God will judge his enemies.

*Study note:* According to the psalm superscription David wrote the psalm while in the “wilderness of Judah.” Perhaps this refers to the period described in {{1 Samuel 23|1 Sam 23-24}} or to the incident mentioned in {{2 Samuel 15:23|2 Sam 15:23}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “I will seek you.”

*Translator's note:* Or “I thirst.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “faint” or “weary.” This may picture the land as “faint” or “weary,” or it may allude to the effect this dry desert has on those who are forced to live in it.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew particle כֵּן (ken) is used here to stress the following affirmation (see {{Joshua 2:4|Josh 2:4}}).

*Translator's note:* The perfect verbal form is understood here as referring to a past experience which the psalmist desires to be repeated. Another option is to take the perfect as indicating the psalmist’s certitude that he will again stand in God’s presence in the sanctuary. In this case one can translate, “I will see you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “seeing.” The preposition with the infinitive construct here indicates an accompanying circumstance.

*Translator's note:* This line is understood as giving the basis for the praise promised in the following line. Another option is to take the Hebrew particle כִּי (ki) as asseverative/emphasizing, “Indeed, your loyal love is better” (cf. NEB, which leaves the particle untranslated).

*Translator's note:* The word “experiencing” is supplied in the translation for clarification. The psalmist does not speak here of divine loyal love in some abstract sense, but of loyal love revealed and experienced.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “then.”

*Study note:* *I will lift up my hands*. Lifting up one’s hands toward God was a gesture of prayer (see {{Psalm 28:2|Ps 28:2}}; Lam 2:19) or respect ({{Psalm 119:48|Ps 119:48}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like fat and fatness.”

*Translator's note:* Or “me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [with] lips of joy my mouth praises.”
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term אִם (ʾim) is used here in the sense of “when; whenever,” as in {{Psalm 78:34|Ps 78:34}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “[source of] help.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the shadow of your wings.”

*Translator's note:* Or “I.” The Hebrew term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) with a pronominal suffix is often equivalent to a pronoun, especially in poetry (see BDB 660 s.v. נֶפֶשׁ 4.a).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “clings after.” The expression means “to pursue with determination” (see {{Judges 20:45|Judg 20:45}}; {{1 Samuel 14:22|1 Sam 14:22}}; 1 Chr 10:2; Jer 42:16).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but they for destruction seek my life.” The pronoun “they” must refer here to the psalmist’s enemies, referred to at this point for the first time in the psalm.

*Study note:* *The depths of the earth* refers here to the underworld dwelling place of the dead (see {{Ezekiel 26:20|Ezek 26:20}}; {{Ezekiel 31:14|31:14}}, {{Ezekiel 31:16|16}}, {{Ezekiel 31:18|18}}; {{Ezekiel 32:18|32:18}}, {{Ezekiel 32:24|24}}). See L. I. J. Stadelmann, *The Hebrew Conception of the World*, 167.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they will deliver him over to the sword.” The third masculine plural subject must be indefinite (see GKC 460 §144.*f*) and the singular pronominal suffix either representative or distributive (emphasizing that each one will be so treated). Active verbs with indefinite subjects may be translated as passives with the object (in the Hebrew text) as subject (in the translation).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they will be [the] portion of jackals”; traditionally, “of foxes.”

*Study note:* The psalmist probably refers to himself in the third person here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who swears [an oath] by him.”

*Translator's note:* The Niphal of this verb occurs only here and in {{Genesis 8:2|Gen 8:2}}, where it is used of God “stopping” or “damming up” the great deep as he brought the flood to an end.

*Study note:* *Psalm 64*. The psalmist asks God to protect him from his dangerous enemies and then confidently affirms that God will destroy his enemies and demonstrate his justice in the sight of all observers.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my voice.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form is used here to express the psalmist’s request.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the terror of [the] enemy.” “Terror” is used here metonymically for the enemy’s attacks that produce fear because they threaten the psalmist’s life.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who.” A new sentence was started here in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a bitter word.”

*Translator's note:* The psalmist uses the singular because he is referring to himself here as representative of a larger group.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and are unafraid.” The words “of retaliation” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they give strength to themselves, an evil matter [or “word”].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they report about hiding.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they say.”

*Translator's note:* If this is a direct quotation (cf. NASB, NIV), the pronoun “them” refers to the snares mentioned in the previous line. If it is an indirect quotation, then the pronoun may refer to the enemies themselves (cf. NEB, which is ambiguous). Some translations retain the direct quotation but alter the pronoun to “us,” referring clearly to the enemies (cf. NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “search out, examine,” which here means (by metonymy) “devise.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT has תַּמְנוּ (tamnu, “we are finished”), a Qal perfect first common plural form from the verbal root תָּמַם (tamam). Some understand this as the beginning of a quotation of the enemies’ words and translate, “we have completed,” but the Hiphil would seem to be required in this case. The present translation follows many medieval Hebrew mss in reading טָמְנוּ (tamenu, “they hide”), a Qal perfect third common plural form from the verbal root טָמַן (taman).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a searched-out search,” which is understood as referring here to a thoroughly planned plot to destroy the psalmist.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the inner part of man, and a heart [is] deep.” The point seems to be that a man’s inner thoughts are incapable of being discovered. No one is a mind reader! Consequently the psalmist is vulnerable to his enemies’ well-disguised plots.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verb with vav (ו) consecutive is normally used in narrative contexts to describe completed past actions. It is possible that the conclusion to the psalm (vv. {{Psalm 64:7|7-10}}) was added to the lament after God’s judgment of the wicked in response to the psalmist’s lament (vv. {{Psalm 64:1|1-6}}). The translation assumes that these verses are anticipatory and express the psalmist’s confidence that God would eventually judge the wicked. The psalmist uses a narrative style as a rhetorical device to emphasize his certitude. See GKC 329-30 §111.*w*.

*Translator's note:* The perfect verbal form here expresses the psalmist’s certitude about the coming demise of the wicked.

*Translator's note:* The translation follows the traditional accentuation of the MT. Another option is to translate, “But God will shoot them down with an arrow, suddenly they will be wounded” (cf. NIV, NRSV).

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads literally, “and they caused him [or it] to stumble upon them, their tongue.” Perhaps the third plural subject of the verb is indefinite with the third singular pronominal suffix on the verb being distributive (see {{Psalm 63:10|Ps 63:10}}). In this case one may translate, “each one will be made to stumble.” The preposition עַל (ʿal) might then be taken as adversative, “against them [is] their tongue.” Many prefer to emend the text to וַיַּכְשִׁילֵמוֹ עֲלֵי לְשׁוֹנָם (vayyakhshilemo ʿale leshonam, “and he caused them to stumble over their tongue”). However, if this reading is original, it is difficult to see how the present reading of the MT arose. Furthermore, the preposition is not collocated with the verb כָּשַׁל (kashal) elsewhere. Perhaps a better option is that the third singular pronominal suffix “it” refers to the following noun “tongue” translated “they caused it, their tongue, to stumble on themselves” (see GKC 425-26 §131.*m*, *o*).

*Translator's note:* The Hitpolel verbal form is probably from the root נוּד (nud; see *HALOT* 678 s.v. נוד), which is attested elsewhere in the Hitpolel stem, not the root נָדַד (nadad, as proposed by BDB 622 s.v. I נָדַד), which does not occur elsewhere in this stem.

*Text-critical note:* Many medieval Hebrew mss read וַיִּרְאוּ (vayyirʾu, “and they will see”) instead of וַיִּירְאוּ (vayyireʾu, “and they will fear”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the work of God,” referring to the judgment described in v. {{Psalm 64:7|7}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “upright in heart.”

*Translator's note:* That is, about the Lord’s accomplishments on their behalf.

*Study note:* *Psalm 65*. The psalmist praises God because he forgives sin and blesses his people with an abundant harvest.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for you, silence, praise.” Many prefer to emend the noun דֻּמִיָּה (dumiyyah, “silence”) to a participle דּוֹמִיָּה (domiyyah), from the root דָּמָה (damah, “be silent”), understood here in the sense of “wait.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O one who hears prayer.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to you all flesh comes.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the records of sins are too strong for me.”

*Translator's note:* Or “make atonement for.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see {{Psalm 1:1|Pss 1:1}}; {{Psalm 2:12|2:12}}; {{Psalm 34:9|34:9}}; {{Psalm 41:1|41:1}}; {{Psalm 84:12|84:12}}; {{Psalm 89:15|89:15}}; {{Psalm 106:3|106:3}}; {{Psalm 112:1|112:1}}; {{Psalm 127:5|127:5}}; {{Psalm 128:1|128:1}}; {{Psalm 144:15|144:15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[whom] you bring near [so that] he might live [in] your courts.”

*Translator's note:* Or “temple.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[with] awesome acts in deliverance you answer us, O God of our salvation.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a source of confidence [for] all the ends of the earth.”

*Study note:* *All the ends of the earth trust in you*. This idealistic portrayal of universal worship is typical hymnic hyperbole, though it does anticipate eschatological reality.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and [the] distant sea.” The plural adjective is problematic after the singular form “sea.” One could emend יָם (yam, “sea”) to יָמִים (yamim, “seas”), or emend the plural form רְחֹקִים (rekhoqim, “far”) to the singular רָחֹק (rakhoq). In this case the final mem (ם) could be treated as dittographic; note the *mem* on the beginning of the first word in v. {{Psalm 65:6|6}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the] one who establishes [the] mountains by his power.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one [who] is girded with strength”; or “one [who] girds himself with strength.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the roar of the seas.”

*Study note:* *The raging seas…the commotion made by the nations*. The raging seas symbolize the turbulent nations of the earth (see {{Psalm 46:2|Ps 46:2-3}}, {{Psalm 46:6|6}}; {{Isaiah 17:12|Isa 17:12}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the inhabitants of the ends fear because of your signs.” God’s “signs” are the “awesome acts” (see v. {{Psalm 65:5|5}}) he performs in the earth.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the goings out of the morning and the evening you cause to shout for joy.” The phrase “goings out of the morning and evening” refers to the sunrise and sunset, that is, the east and the west.

*Translator's note:* The verb form is a Polel from שׁוּק (shuq, “be abundant”), a verb which appears only here and in Joel 2:24 and 3:13, where it is used in the Hiphil stem and means “overflow.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you greatly enrich it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[with] a channel of God full of water.” The divine name is probably may be used here in a superlative sense to depict a very deep stream (“a stream fit for God,” as it were).

*Translator's note:* The pronoun apparently refers to the people of the earth, mentioned in v. {{Psalm 65:8|8}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for thus [referring to the provision of rain described in the first half of the verse] you prepare it.” The third feminine singular pronominal suffix attached to the verb “prepare” refers back to the “earth,” which is a feminine noun with regard to grammatical form.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “saturating” [the form is an infinitive absolute].

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “flatten, cause to sink.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “trenches,” or “furrows.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “soften it,” that is, the earth.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “its vegetation you bless.” Divine “blessing” often involves endowing an object with special power or capacity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your good,” which refers here to agricultural blessings.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and your paths drip with abundance.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “drip.”

*Translator's note:* That is, with rich vegetation that brings joy to those who see it.
*Study note:* *Psalm 66*. The psalmist praises God because he has delivered his people from a crisis.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his name,” which here stands metonymically for God’s reputation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “make honorable his praise.”

*Translator's note:* See {{Deuteronomy 33:29|Deut 33:29}}; {{Psalm 81:15|Ps 81:15}} for other uses of the verb כָּחַשׁ (kakhash) in the sense “cower in fear.” In {{Psalm 18:44|Ps 18:44}} the verb seems to carry the nuance “be weak, powerless” (see also {{Psalm 109:24|Ps 109:24}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “bows down to.” The prefixed verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 66:4|4}} are taken (1) as imperfects expressing what is typical. Another option (2) is to interpret them as anticipatory (“all the earth will worship you”) or (3) take them as jussives, expressing a prayer or wish (“may all the earth worship you”).

*Translator's note:* Or “see.”

*Translator's note:* Or “acts” (see {{Psalm 46:8|Ps 46:8}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “awesome [is] an act toward the sons of man.” It is unclear how the prepositional phrase relates to what precedes. If collocated with “act,” it may mean “on behalf of” or “toward.” If taken with “awesome” (see 1 Chr 16:25; {{Psalm 89:7|Pss 89:7}}; {{Psalm 96:4|96:4}}; Zeph 2:11), one might translate “his awesome acts are beyond human comprehension” or “his awesome acts are superior to anything men can do.”

*Study note:* *He turned the sea into dry land*. The psalmist alludes to Israel’s crossing the Red Sea ({{Exodus 14:21|Exod 14:21}}).

*Translator's note:* Because of the reference to “the river,” some understand this as an allusion to Israel’s crossing the Jordan River. However, the Hebrew term נָהָר (nahad) does not always refer to a “river” in the technical sense; it can be used of sea currents (see {{Jonah 2:4|Jonah 2:4}}). So this line may also refer to the Red Sea crossing (cf. NEB).

*Translator's note:* The adverb שָׁם (sham, “there”) is used here, as often in poetic texts, to point “to a spot in which a scene is localized vividly in the imagination” (BDB 1027 s.v.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the] one who rules.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his eyes watch.” “Eyes” are an anthropomorphism, attributed to God here to emphasize his awareness of all that happens on earth.

*Translator's note:* The verb form is jussive (note the negative particle אַל, ʾal). The *Kethib* (consonantal text) has a Hiphil form of the verb, apparently to be understood in an exhibitive sense (“demonstrate stubborn rebellion”; see BDB 927 s.v. רוּם Hiph), while the *Qere* (marginal reading) has a Qal form, to be understood in an intransitive sense. The preposition ל (lamed) with pronominal suffix should be understood in a reflexive sense (“for themselves”) and indicates that the action is performed with the interest of the subject in mind.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bless,” in the sense of declaring “God to be the source of…special power” (see *HALOT* 160 s.v. II ברך pi).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cause the voice of his praise to be heard.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who places our soul in life.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you brought us into a net.” This rare word for “net” also occurs in {{Ezekiel 12:13|Ezek 12:13}}; {{Ezekiel 13:21|13:21}}; {{Ezekiel 17:20|17:20}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you placed suffering on our hips.” The noun מוּעָקָה (muʿaqah, “suffering”) occurs only here in the OT.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads רְוָיָה (revayah, “saturation”) but this should be emended to רְוָחָה (revakhah, “wide open place”; i.e., “relief”), a reading supported by several ancient versions (LXX, Syriac, Jerome, Targum).
*Study note:* Here the psalmist switches to the singular; he speaks as the representative of the nation.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all of the fearers of God.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to him [with] my mouth I called.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he was extolled under my tongue.” The form רוֹמַם (romam) appears to be a Polal (passive) participle from רוּם (rum, “be exalted”), but many prefer to read רוֹמָם, “high praise [was under my tongue]” (cf. NEB). See BDB 928 s.v. רוֹמָם.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sin if I had seen in my heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “blessed [be] God.”

*Translator's note:* Or “who.” In a blessing formula after בָּרוּךְ (barukh, “blessed be”) the form אֲשֶׁר (ʾasher), whether taken as a relative pronoun or causal particle, introduces the basis for the blessing/praise.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “did not turn aside my prayer, or his loyal love from with me.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 67*. The psalmist prays for God’s blessing upon his people and urges the nations to praise him for he is the just ruler of the world.

*Translator's note:* Or “have mercy on us.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal forms are understood as jussives expressing the psalmist’s prayer. Note the jussive form יָאֵר (yaʾer) in the next line.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may he cause his face to shine with us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to know in the earth your way, among all nations your deliverance.” The infinitive with ל (lamed) expresses purpose/result. When God demonstrates his favor to his people, all nations will recognize his character as a God who delivers. The Hebrew term דֶּרֶךְ (derekh, “way”) refers here to God’s characteristic behavior, more specifically, to the way he typically saves his people.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let the nations, all of them, thank you.” The prefixed verbal forms in vv. {{Psalm 67:3|3-4a}} are understood as jussives in this call to praise.

*Translator's note:* Or “peoples.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for you judge nations fairly, and [as for the] peoples in the earth, you lead them.” The imperfects are translated with the present tense because the statement is understood as a generalization about God’s providential control of the world. Another option is to understand the statement as anticipating God’s future rule (“for you will rule…and govern”).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let the nations, all of them, thank you.” The prefixed verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 67:5|5}} are understood as jussives in this call to praise.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verb forms in vv. {{Psalm 67:6|6b-7a}} are understood as jussives.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will fear him.” After the jussive of the preceding line, the prefixed verbal form with prefixed vav (ו) conjunctive is understood as indicating purpose/result. (Note how v. {{Psalm 67:3|3}} anticipates the universal impact of God showing his people blessing.) Another option is to take the verb as a jussive and translate, “Let all the ends of the earth fear him.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 68*. The psalmist depicts God as a mighty warrior and celebrates the fact that God exerts his power on behalf of his people.

*Translator's note:* Or “rises up.” The verb form is an imperfect, not a jussive. The psalmist is describing God’s appearance in battle in a dramatic fashion.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who hate him.”

*Study note:* The wording of v. {{Psalm 68:1|1}} echoes the prayer in {{Numbers 10:35|Num 10:35}}: “Spring into action, Lord. Then your enemies will be scattered and your adversaries will run from you.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “as smoke is scattered, you scatter [them].”

*Translator's note:* By placing the subject first the psalmist highlights the contrast between God’s ecstatic people and his defeated enemies (vv. {{Psalm 68:1|1-2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they are happy with joy” (cf. NEB). Some translate the prefixed verbal forms of v. {{Psalm 68:3|3}} as jussives, “Let the godly be happy, let them rejoice before God, and let them be happy with joy!” (Cf. NASB, NIV, NRSV; note the call to praise in v. {{Psalm 68:4|4}}.)

*Translator's note:* Traditionally the Hebrew term עֲרָבוֹת (ʿaravot) is taken as “steppe-lands” (often rendered “deserts”), but here the form is probably a homonym meaning “clouds.” Verse {{Psalm 68:33|33}}, which depicts God as the one who “rides on the sky” strongly favors this (see as well {{Deuteronomy 33:26|Deut 33:26}}), as does the reference in v. {{Psalm 68:9|9}} to God as the source of rain. The term עֲרָבָה (ʿaravah, “cloud”) is cognate with Akkadian urpatu*/*erpetu and with Ugaritic ʿrpt. The phrase rkb ʿrpt (“one who rides on the clouds”) appears in Ugaritic mythological texts as an epithet of the storm god Baal. The nonphonemic interchange of the bilabial consonants b and p is attested elsewhere in roots common to Hebrew and Ugaritic, though the phenomenon is relatively rare.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “in the Lord his name.” If the MT is retained, the preposition ב (bet) is introducing the predicate (the so-called bet of identity), “the Lord is his name.” However, some prefer to emend the text to כִּי יָהּ שְׁמוֹ (ki yah shemo, “for Yah is his name”). This emendation, reflected in the present translation, assumes a confusion of ב (bet) and כ (kaf) and haplography of י (yod).

*Study note:* God is depicted here as a just ruler. In the ancient Near Eastern world a king was responsible for promoting justice, including caring for the weak and vulnerable, epitomized by the *fatherless* and *widows*.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “God [is] in his holy dwelling place.” He occupies his throne and carries out his royal responsibilities.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “God causes the solitary ones to dwell in a house.” The participle suggests this is what God typically does.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he brings out prisoners into prosperity.” Another option is to translate, “he brings out prisoners with singing” (cf. NIV). The participle suggests this is what God typically does.

*Translator's note:* Or “in a parched [land].”

*Study note:* God delivers the downtrodden and oppressed, but *sinful rebels* who oppose his reign are treated appropriately.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when you go out before your people.” The Hebrew idiom “go out before” is used here in a militaristic sense of leading troops into battle (see {{Judges 4:14|Judg 4:14}}; {{Judges 9:39|9:39}}; {{2 Samuel 5:24|2 Sam 5:24}}).

*Study note:* *When you march through the wastelands*. Some interpreters think that v. {{Psalm 68:7|7}} alludes to Israel’s exodus from Egypt and its subsequent travels in the wilderness. Another option is that v. {{Psalm 68:7|7}}, like v. {{Psalm 68:8|8}}, echoes {{Judges 5:4|Judg 5:4}}, which describes how the God of Sinai marched across the plains of Edom to do battle with Sisera and his Canaanite army.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this one of Sinai.” The phrase is a divine title, perhaps indicating that the Lord rules from Sinai.

*Study note:* The language of vv. {{Psalm 68:7|7-8}} is reminiscent of {{Judges 5:4|Judg 5:4-5}}, which tells how the God of Sinai came in the storm and annihilated the Canaanite forces led by Sisera. The presence of allusion does not mean, however, that this is a purely historical reference. The psalmist is describing God’s typical appearance as a warrior in terms of his prior self-revelation as ancient events are reactualized in the psalmist’s experience. (For a similar literary technique, see {{Habakkuk 3|Hab 3}}.)

*Translator's note:* The verb נוּף (nuf, “cause rain to fall”) is a homonym of the more common נוּף (“brandish”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[on] your inheritance.” This refers to Israel as God’s specially chosen people (see {{Psalm 28:9|Pss 28:9}}; {{Psalm 33:12|33:12}}; {{Psalm 74:2|74:2}}; {{Psalm 78:62|78:62}}, {{Psalm 78:71|71}}; {{Psalm 79:1|79:1}}; {{Psalm 94:5|94:5}}, {{Psalm 94:14|14}}; {{Psalm 106:40|106:40}}). Some take “your inheritance” with what follows, but the vav (ו) prefixed to the following word (note וְנִלְאָה, venilʾah) makes this syntactically unlikely.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it [is],” referring to God’s “inheritance.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it,” referring to God’s “inheritance.”

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew text is unclear; it appears to read, “your animals, they live in it,” but this makes little, if any, sense in this context. Some suggest that חָיָּה (khayah) is a rare homonym here, meaning “community” (BDB 312 s.v.) or “dwelling place” (*HALOT* 310 s.v. III *הַיָּה). In this case one may take “your community/dwelling place” as appositional to the third feminine singular pronominal suffix at the end of v. {{Psalm 68:9|9}}, the antecedent of which is “your inheritance.” The phrase יָשְׁבוּ־בָהּ (yashevu vah, “they live in it”) may then be understood as an asyndetic relative clause modifying “your community/dwelling place.” A literal translation of vv. {{Psalm 68:9|9b-10a}} would be, “when it [your inheritance] is tired, you sustain it, your community/dwelling place in [which] they live.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “gives a word.” Perhaps this refers to a divine royal decree or battle cry.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the ones spreading the good news [are] a large army.” The participle translated “the ones spreading the good news” is a feminine plural form. Apparently the good news here is the announcement that enemy kings have been defeated (see v. {{Psalm 68:12|12}}).

*Translator's note:* The verbal repetition draws attention to the statement.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew form appears to be the construct of נוּה (nuh, “pasture”) but the phrase “pasture of the house” makes no sense here. The translation assumes that the form is an alternative or textual variation of נאוה (“beautiful woman”). A reference to a woman would be appropriate in light of v. {{Psalm 68:11|11b}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “if.”

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew word translated “sheepfolds” is uncertain. There may be an echo of {{Judges 5:16|Judg 5:16}} here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and her pinions with the yellow of gold.”

*Study note:* The point of the imagery of v. {{Psalm 68:13|13}} is not certain, though the reference to *silver* and *gold* appears to be positive. Both would be part of the loot carried away from battle (see v. {{Psalm 68:12|12b}}).

*Translator's note:* The divine name used here is שַׁדַּי (“Shaddai”). Shaddai/El Shaddai is the sovereign king/judge of the world who grants life, blesses and kills, and judges. In Genesis he blesses the patriarchs with fertility and promises numerous descendants. Outside Genesis he both blesses (protects) and takes away life and/or happiness.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text adds “in it.” The third feminine singular pronominal suffix may refer back to God’s community/dwelling place (v. {{Psalm 68:10|10}}).

*Study note:* *Zalmon* was apparently a mountain in the region, perhaps the one mentioned in {{Judges 9:46|Judg 9:46}} as being in the vicinity of Shechem.

*Translator's note:* The verb form appears to be a Hiphil jussive from שָׁלַג (shalag), which is usually understood as a denominative verb from שֶׁלֶג (sheleg, “snow”) with an indefinite subject. The form could be taken as a preterite, in which case one might translate, “when the sovereign judge scattered kings, it snowed on Zalmon” (cf. NIV, NRSV). The point of the image is unclear. Perhaps “snow” suggests fertility and blessing (see v. {{Psalm 68:9|9}} and {{Isaiah 55:10|Isa 55:10}}), or the image of a snow-capped mountain suggests grandeur.

*Study note:* The *mountain of Bashan* probably refers to Mount Hermon.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a mountain of God.” The divine name is probably used here in a superlative sense to depict a very high mountain (“a mountain fit for God,” as it were). Cf. NIV11 “majestic mountain”; NRSV “O mighty mountain.”

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew term, which appears only here in the OT, is uncertain. *HALOT* 174 s.v. גַּבְנוֹן suggests “many-peaked,” while BDB 148 s.v. גַּבְנִן suggests “rounded summit.”

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew verb רָצַד (ratsad), translated here “look with envy,” is uncertain; it occurs only here in the OT. See BDB 952-53. A cognate verb occurs in later Aramaic with the meaning “to lie in wait; to watch” (Jastrow 1492 s.v. רְצַד).

*Translator's note:* Perhaps the apparent plural form should be read as a singular with enclitic mem (ם; later misinterpreted as a plural ending). The preceding verse has the singular form.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[at] the mountain God desires for his dwelling place.” The reference is to Mount Zion/Jerusalem.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew particle אַף (ʾaf) has an emphasizing function here.

*Translator's note:* The word “there” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “thousands of [?].” The meaning of the word שִׁנְאָן (shinʾan), which occurs only here in the OT, is uncertain. Perhaps the form should be emended to שַׁאֲנָן (shaʾanan, “at ease”) and be translated here “held in reserve.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads, “the Lord [is] among them, Sinai, in holiness,” which is syntactically difficult. The present translation assumes an emendation to אֲדֹנָי בָּא מִסִּינַי (ʾadonay baʾ missinay; see *BHS* note b-b and {{Deuteronomy 33:2|Deut 33:2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the elevated place”; or “on high.” This probably refers to the Lord’s throne on Mount Zion.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you have taken captives captive.”

*Translator's note:* Or “gifts.”

*Translator's note:* Or “among.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so that the Lord God might live [there].” Many take the infinitive construct with ל (lamed) as indicating purpose here, but it is unclear how the offering of tribute enables the Lord to live in Zion. This may be an occurrence of the relatively rare emphatic lamed (see *HALOT* 510-11 s.v. II לְ, though this text is not listed as an example there). If so, the statement corresponds nicely to the final line of v. {{Psalm 68:16|16}}, which also affirms emphatically that the Lord lives in Zion.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “blessed [be] the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* It is possible to take this phrase with what precedes (“The Lord deserves praise day after day”) rather than with what follows.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and to the Lord, the Lord, to death, goings out.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the hairy forehead of the one who walks about in his guilt.” The singular is representative.
*Translator's note:* That is, the enemies mentioned in v. {{Psalm 68:21|21}}. Even if they retreat to distant regions, God will retrieve them and make them taste his judgment.

*Text-critical note:* Some (e.g. NRSV) prefer to emend מָחַץ (makhats, “smash; stomp”; see v. {{Psalm 68:21|21}}) to רָחַץ (rakhats, “bathe”; see {{Psalm 58:10|Ps 58:10}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[and] the tongue of your dogs from [the] enemies [may eat] its portion.”

*Translator's note:* The subject is probably indefinite, referring to bystanders in general who witness the procession.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has simply “in holiness.” The words “who marches along” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “after [are] the stringed instrument players.”

*Study note:* To celebrate a military victory, women would play *tambourines* (see {{Exodus 15:20|Exod 15:20}}; {{Judges 11:34|Judg 11:34}}; {{1 Samuel 18:6|1 Sam 18:6}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the fountain of Israel,” which makes little, if any, sense here. The translation assumes an emendation to בְּמִקְרָאֵי (bemiqraʾe, “in the assemblies of [Israel]”).

*Study note:* *Little Benjamin, their ruler*. This may allude to the fact that Israel’s first king, Saul, was from the tribe of Benjamin.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads רִגְמָתָם (rigmatam), which many derive from רָגַם (ragam, “to kill by stoning”) and translates, “[in] their heaps,” that is, in large numbers. One Hebrew ms and Jerome’s *iuxta Hebraeos* (*“in purpura sua”*) support “robes.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “God has commanded your strength.” The statement is apparently addressed to Israel (see v. {{Psalm 68:26|26}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Be strong, O God, [you] who have acted for us, from your temple in Jerusalem.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb גָּעַר (gaʿar) is often understood to mean “rebuke.” In some cases it is apparent that scolding or threatening is in view (see {{Genesis 37:10|Gen 37:10}}; {{Ruth 2:16|Ruth 2:16}}; Zech 3:2). However, in militaristic contexts such as {{Psalm 68|Ps 68}} this translation is inadequate, for the verb refers in this setting to the warrior’s battle cry, which terrifies and paralyzes the enemy. See A. Caquot, *TDOT* 3:53, and note the use of the verb in {{Psalm 106:9|Ps 106:9}} and Nah 1:4, as well as the related noun in {{Job 26:11|Job 26:11}}; {{Psalm 18:15|Pss 18:15}}; {{Psalm 76:6|76:6}}; {{Psalm 104:7|104:7}}; {{Isaiah 50:2|Isa 50:2}}; {{Isaiah 51:20|51:20}}; {{Isaiah 66:15|66:15}}.

*Study note:* *The wild beast of the reeds* probably refers to a hippopotamus, which in turn symbolizes the nation of Egypt.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “an assembly of bulls, with calves of the nations.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “humbling himself.” The verb form is a Hitpael participle from the root רָפַס (rafas, “to trample”). The Hitpael of this verb appears only here and in {{Proverbs 6:3|Prov 6:3}}, where it seems to mean, “humble oneself,” a nuance that fits nicely in this context. The apparent subject is “wild beast” or “assembly,” though both of these nouns are grammatically feminine, while the participle is a masculine form. Perhaps one should emend the participial form to a masculine plural (מִתְרַפִּם, mitrappim) and understand “bulls” or “calves” as the subject.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “with pieces [?] of silver.” The meaning of the Hebrew term רַצֵּי (ratse) is unclear. It is probably best to emend the text to בֶּצֶר וְכָסֶף (betser vekhasef, “[with] gold and silver”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The verb בָּזַר (bazar) is an alternative form of פָּזַר (pazar, “scatter”).

*Translator's note:* This noun, which occurs only here in the OT, apparently means “red cloth” or “bronze articles” (see *HALOT* 362 s.v. חַשְׁמַן; cf. NEB “tribute”). Traditionally the word has been taken to refer to “nobles” (see BDB 365 s.v. חַשְׁמַן; cf. NIV “envoys”). Another option would be to emend the text to הַשְׁמַנִּים (hashmannim, “the robust ones,” i.e., leaders).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Cush.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “causes its hands to run,” which must mean “quickly stretches out its hands” (to present tribute).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “to the one who rides through the skies of skies of ancient times.” If the MT is retained, one might translate, “to the one who rides through the ancient skies.” (שְׁמֵי [sheme, “skies of”] may be accidentally repeated.) The present translation assumes an emendation to בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִקֶּדֶם (bashamayim miqqedem, “[to the one who rides] through the sky from ancient times”), that is, God has been revealing his power through the storm since ancient times.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he gives his voice, a strong voice.” In this context God’s “voice” is the thunder that accompanies the rain (see vv. {{Psalm 68:8|8-9}}, as well as {{Deuteronomy 33:26|Deut 33:26}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “give strength to God.”

*Study note:* The language of v. {{Psalm 68:34|34}} echoes that of {{Deuteronomy 33:26|Deut 33:26}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “awesome [is] God from his holy places.” The plural of מִקְדָּשׁ (miqdash, “holy places”) perhaps refers to the temple precincts (see {{Psalm 73:17|Ps 73:17}}; Jer 51:51).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the God of Israel, he.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “blessed [be] God.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 69*. The psalmist laments his oppressed condition and asks the Lord to deliver him by severely judging his enemies.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to lilies.” See the superscription to {{Psalm 45|Ps 45}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) here refers to the psalmist’s throat or neck. The psalmist compares himself to a helpless, drowning man.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and there is no place to stand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “have entered.”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “raw”; *Heb* “burned; inflamed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my eyes fail from waiting for my God.” The psalmist has intently kept his eyes open, looking for God to intervene, but now his eyes are watery and bloodshot, impairing his vision.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[with] a lie.” The Hebrew noun שֶׁקֶר (sheqer, “lie”) is used here as an adverb, “falsely, wrongfully” (see {{Psalm 35:19|Pss 35:19}}; {{Psalm 38:19|38:19}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb עָצַם (ʿatsam) can sometimes mean “are strong,” but here it probably focuses on numerical superiority; note the parallel verb רָבַב (ravav, “be many”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that which I did not steal, then I restore.” Apparently אָז (ʾaz, “then”) is used here to emphasize the verb that follows.

*Study note:* *They make me repay what I did not steal*. The psalmist’s enemies falsely accuse him and hold him accountable for alleged crimes he did not even commit.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you know my foolishness.”

*Study note:* The psalmist is the first to admit that he is not perfect. But even so, he is innocent of the allegations which his enemies bring against him (v. {{Psalm 69:5|5b}}). God, who is aware of his *foolish sins* and *guilt*, can testify to the truth of his claim.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O Lord Yahweh of hosts.” Both titles draw attention to God’s sovereign position.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “carry, bear.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “on account of you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and shame covers my face.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I am estranged to my brothers, and a foreigner to the sons of my mother.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.” This verse explains that the psalmist’s suffering is due to his allegiance to God.

*Translator's note:* Or “devotion to.”

*Study note:* God’s *house*, the temple, here represents by metonymy God himself.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the insults of those who insult you fall upon me.”

*Study note:* {{John 2:17|Jn 2:17}} applies the first half of this verse to Jesus’ ministry in the context of John’s account of Jesus cleansing the temple.

*Study note:* Fasting was a practice of mourners. By refraining from normal activities such as *eating food*, the mourner demonstrated the sincerity of his sorrow.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and it becomes insults to me.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I am an object of ridicule to them.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the mocking songs of the drinkers of beer.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “as for me, [may] my prayer be to you, O Lord, [in] a time of favor.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O God, in the abundance of your loyal love, answer me in the faithfulness of your deliverance.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “well,” which here symbolizes the place of the dead (cf. {{Psalm 55:23|Ps 55:23}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not let the well close its mouth upon me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not hide your face from.” The Hebrew idiom “hide the face” can (1) mean “ignore” (see {{Psalm 10:11|Pss 10:11}}; {{Psalm 13:1|13:1}}; {{Psalm 51:9|51:9}}) or (2) carry the stronger idea of “reject” (see {{Psalm 30:7|Pss 30:7}}; {{Psalm 88:14|88:14}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “quickly.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “come near my life and redeem it.” The verb “redeem” casts the Lord in the role of a leader who protects members of his extended family in times of need and crisis (see {{Psalm 19:14|Ps 19:14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “break my heart.” The “heart” is viewed here as the origin of the psalmist’s emotions.

*Translator's note:* The verb form appears to be a Qal preterite from an otherwise unattested root נוּשׁ (nush), which some consider an alternate form of אָנַשׁ (ʾanash, “be weak; be sick”; see BDB 60 s.v. I אָנַשׁ). Perhaps the form should be emended to a Niphal, וָאֵאָנְשָׁה (vaʾeʾaneshah, “and I am sick”). The Niphal of אָנַשׁ occurs in {{2 Samuel 12:15|2 Sam 12:15}}, where it is used to describe David’s sick child.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wait.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I wait for sympathy, but there is none.” The form נוּד (nud) is an infinitive functioning as a verbal noun:, “sympathizing.” Some suggest emending the form to a participle נָד (nad, “one who shows sympathy”). The verb נוּד (nud) also has the nuance “show sympathy” in {{Job 2:11|Job 2:11}}; {{Job 42:11|42:11}} and {{Isaiah 51:19|Isa 51:19}}.

*Translator's note:* According to BDB 912 s.v. II רֹאשׁ the term can mean “a bitter and poisonous plant.”

*Study note:* {{John 19:28|John 19:28-30}} appears to understand Jesus’ experience on the cross as a fulfillment of this passage (or {{Psalm 22:15|Ps 22:15}}). See the study note on the word “thirsty” in {{John 19:28|John 19:28}}.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and to the friends for a snare.” The plural of שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace”) is used in {{Psalm 55:20|Ps 55:20}} of one’s “friends.” If the reading of the MT is retained here, the term depicts the psalmist’s enemies as a close-knit group of friends who are bound together by their hatred for the psalmist. Some prefer to revocalize the text as וּלְשִׁלּוּמִים (uleshillumim, “and for retribution”). In this case the noun stands parallel to פַּח (pakh, “trap”) and מוֹקֵשׁ (moqesh, “snare”), and one might translate, “may their dining table become a trap before them, [a means of] retribution and a snare” (cf. NIV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may their eyes be darkened from seeing.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “make their hips shake continually.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “anger.” “Anger” here refers metonymically to divine judgment, which is the practical effect of God’s anger.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the rage of your anger.” The phrase “rage of your anger” employs an appositional genitive. Synonyms are joined in a construct relationship to emphasize the single idea. For a detailed discussion of the grammatical point with numerous examples, see Y. Avishur, “Pairs of Synonymous Words in the Construct State (and in Appositional Hendiadys) in Biblical Hebrew,” *Semitics* 2 (1971), 17-81.

*Study note:* In {{Acts 1:20|Acts 1:20}} Peter applies the language of this verse to Judas’ experience. By changing the pronouns from plural to singular, he is able to apply the ancient curse, pronounced against the psalmist’s enemies, to Judas in particular.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in their tents may there not be one who dwells.”

*Translator's note:* Or “persecute”; *Heb* “chase.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for you, the one whom you strike, they chase.”

*Study note:* The psalmist is innocent of the false charges made by his enemies (v. {{Psalm 69:4|4}}), but he is also aware of his sinfulness (v. {{Psalm 69:5|5}}) and admits that he experiences divine *discipline* (v. {{Psalm 69:26|26}}) despite his devotion to God (v. {{Psalm 69:9|9}}). Here he laments that his enemies take advantage of such divine discipline by harassing and slandering him. They “kick him while he’s down,” as the expression goes.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they announce the pain of your wounded ones” (i.e., “the ones whom you wounded,” as the parallel line makes clear).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “place sin upon their sin.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let them not come into your vindication.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let them be wiped out of the scroll of the living.”

*Study note:* The phrase *the scroll of the living* occurs only here in the OT. It pictures a scroll or census list containing the names of the citizens of a community. When an individual died, that person’s name was removed from the list. So this curse is a very vivid way of asking that the enemies die.

*Study note:* *Do not let their names be listed with the godly*. This curse pictures a scroll in which God records the names of his loyal followers. The psalmist makes the point that his enemies have no right to be included in this list of the godly.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and with the godly let them not be written.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your deliverance, O God, may it protect me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will praise the name of God with a song.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will magnify him with thanks.”

*Study note:* *You who seek God* refers to those who seek to have a relationship with God by obeying and worshiping him (see {{Psalm 53:2|Ps 53:2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may your heart[s] live.” See {{Psalm 22:26|Ps 22:26}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his prisoners he does not despise.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they”; the referent (God’s people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it.” The third feminine singular pronominal suffix probably refers to “Zion” (see {{Psalm 48:12|Pss 48:12}}; {{Psalm 102:14|102:14}}); thus the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the lovers of his name.” The phrase refers to those who are loyal to God (cf. v. {{Psalm 69:35|35}}). See {{Psalm 5:11|Pss 5:11}}; {{Psalm 119:132|119:132}}; {{Isaiah 56:6|Isa 56:6}}.

*Study note:* Verses {{Psalm 69:35|35-36}} appear to be an addition to the psalm from the time of the exile. The earlier lament reflects an individual’s situation, while these verses seem to reflect a communal application of it.

*Study note:* *Psalm 70*. This psalm is almost identical to Ps 40:13-17. The psalmist asks for God’s help and for divine retribution against his enemies.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to cause to remember.” The same form, a Hiphil infinitive of זָכַר (zakhar, “remember”), also appears in the superscription of {{Psalm 38|Ps 38}}. Some understand this in the sense of “for the memorial offering,” but it may carry the idea of bringing one’s plight to God’s attention (see P. C. Craigie, *{{Psalm 1|Psalms 1-50}}* [WBC], 303).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O God, to rescue me.” A main verb is obviously missing. The verb רָצָה (ratsah, “be willing”) should be supplied (see {{Psalm 40:13|Ps 40:13}}). {{Psalm 40:13|Ps 40:13}} uses the divine name “Lord” rather than “God.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hurry to my help.” See {{Psalm 22:19|Pss 22:19}}; {{Psalm 38:22|38:22}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may they be embarrassed and ashamed, the ones seeking my life.” {{Psalm 40:14|Ps 40:14}} has “together” after “ashamed,” and “to snatch it away” after “my life.”

*Study note:* See {{Psalm 35:4|Ps 35:4}} for a similar prayer.

*Translator's note:* The four prefixed verbal forms in this verse are understood as jussives. The psalmist is calling judgment down on his enemies.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive in this imprecation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “May they be turned back according to their shame, those who say, ‘Aha! Aha!’” {{Psalm 40:15|Ps 40:15}} has the verb “humiliated” instead of “turned back” and adds “to me” after “say.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who love,” which stands metonymically for its cause, the experience of being delivered by God.

*Translator's note:* The three prefixed verbal forms prior to the quotation are understood as jussives. The psalmist balances out his imprecation against his enemies with a prayer of blessing on the godly.

*Translator's note:* {{Psalm 40:16|Ps 40:16}} uses the divine name “Lord” here instead of “God.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive, “may the Lord be magnified [in praise].” Another option is to take the verb as an imperfect, “the Lord is great.” See {{Psalm 35:27|Ps 35:27}}.

*Study note:* See {{Psalm 35:10|Pss 35:10}}; {{Psalm 37:14|37:14}}.

*Translator's note:* {{Psalm 40:17|Ps 40:17}} has “may the Lord pay attention to me.”
